newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian rupiah seen recovering after elections.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian rupiah seen recovering after elections.

text.p: The Indonesian rupiah, jolted briefly on fears of campaign-related unrest, is likely to recover after the May 29 general elections on the back of strong economic fundamentals, economists and currency dealers said.

That view was shared by eight other currency dealers and economists who told Reuters the rupiah's weakness was temporary and the unit would stage a comeback once the dust settles following the month-long campaign, which opened on Sunday.
"There will be a lot of volatility in the next few weeks. But the rupiah will recover after that," said Trisiladi Supriyanto, vice-president of Bank of America in Jakarta.

Said Desmond Supple, head of research for Asian currencies at BZW Barclays in Singapore: "The economy actually suggests the rupiah should strengthen. It's only the political risk which hangs over the currency."
He forecast the rupiah would trade at some 10 to 20 points away from the strong end of the central bank's intervention band, assuming the election does not give rise to instability.
The band allows the bank to intervene if market rates fall outside the daily fixed range. The central bank fixed its intervention band on Friday at 2,404/2,596.
ING Barings economist Daragh Maher said he also expected the rupiah to hover at the lower end of the band in June, based on a steady central bank depreciation policy.
Winston Koh, vice-president for market research at JP Morgan in Singapore, said most people were still comfortable with the long-term view of the rupiah.
"Just at the short-term, they expect there will be some volatility," Koh said, adding that the rupiah would probably be traded at the strong end of the band after the elections.
The rupiah briefly hit an historic low on Friday at 2,440.5 before rebounding to close at 2,434.5/35.5 to the dollar.
It fell 15 points at one stage on Thursday.

The currency's tumble was due to fears of possible unrest during the campaign. The ruling Golkar party is expected to win a comfortable victory in the election, which will proceed without the participation of Indonesia's best-known opposition politician, Megawati Sukarnoputri, the former leader of the Indonesian Democratic Party.

The official electoral commission refused to accept her list of candidates for the polls, and she has called on supporters to boycott the campaign but refrained from calling for an illegal boycott of the vote itself.
Violent clashes between opposing political factions in recent weeks have also heightened tensions.

But economists said the nation's economic fundamentals remain sound, noting the World Bank's recent praise for Indonesia's macroeconomic achievements and efforts to balance fiscal and monetary instruments.
They also pointed to the country's comfortable foreign reserves, which rose steadily to $19.872 billion in March from $15.975 billion in March 1996.
Vincent Low, a JP Morgan economist, said capital inflows to Indonesia were expected to continue, barring political violence.
"The thing that we like particularly about Indonesia is the way that the central bank is handling capital inflows by opting for a more flexible exchange rate," Low said.
